title: Sowing beetroot
subtitle: Direct or module sowing from April for roots from June onwards
excerpt: Beetroot is sown from April to July in the UK for roots from June through October. The seed clusters germinate as groups of seedlings that need thinning. Beetroot bolts if sown in cold ground before the last frost risk has passed.
sourceNotes: Mrs Beeton, Book of Household Management (1861), kitchen garden section. RHS beetroot growing guide (rhs.org.uk). USDA cooperative extension notes on beetroot culture, public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A plant producing a flower stem and setting seed prematurely, before the root or leaf crop has developed. Beetroot bolts if sown into cold soil (below 7°C) or subject to a cold snap after germination. Once the flower stem appears the root becomes woody and unpleasant to eat. Bolt-resistant varieties reduce but don't eliminate the risk.

The corky structure that beetroot seed is contained in. Each cluster holds two to four seeds and produces two to four seedlings. Even 'monogerm' varieties sold as single-seed clusters occasionally produce doubles. Thinning is always needed.

content.text: that usually produces two or three seedlings and needs thinning. Sow from late April to July in the UK for roots from June through October. Early sowing into cold soil risks

Late April is the standard first outdoor sowing in most UK gardens. Bolt-resistant varieties such as Boltardy can go in from late March, but cold spells in April can still trigger bolting. The safest approach is to wait until after the last expected frost date (around mid-April in the south, late May in the north) before sowing. Successional sowings every three weeks through to late June give roots from late June through October.

Full sun or partial shade. Well-drained, reasonably fertile soil. Beetroot grows on most UK soils given reasonable drainage. Avoid very acidic ground (pH below 6.0); lime if needed. A bed with residual fertility from a previous manured crop is fine. Do not add fresh manure directly to the beetroot bed.

Draw drills 2 cm deep and 25 cm apart. Sow seed clusters every 10 cm. Once seedlings are 2 to 3 cm tall, thin to one seedling per cluster, keeping the most vigorous. Final spacing: 10 cm between plants for baby beets, 15 to 20 cm for full-sized roots. Thinnings can be eaten whole as a salad vegetable.

Germination takes one to two weeks at 10 to 20°C. Seedlings emerge as a pair of oval seed leaves on a red-tinged stem. Multiple seedlings at each cluster point are normal; thin promptly to avoid competition. Modules can be used for early sowings: sow two seeds per module, thin to one, and plant out at 10 cm tall.

Water consistently in dry spells once the roots start to develop (visible as a swelling at the base of the stems). Irregular watering causes the roots to split. Mulch between rows with compost or grass clippings to retain moisture. Keep the bed weed-free by hand-weeding close to the plants; hoe carefully between rows.

attrs.heading: Common problems
attrs.intro: The main things that go wrong with beetroot sowing.

items.symptom: Plants produce a tall flower stem early, roots are small and woody
items.cause: Bolting, triggered by cold early sowing or a cold snap after germination.
items.fix: Use bolt-resistant varieties for early sowings. Wait until late April for unprotected outdoor sowing. Cover early sowings with fleece during cold nights in spring.

items.cause: Heavy rain or irrigation after a dry spell, causing rapid growth.
items.fix: Water consistently rather than in large irregular doses. Mulch to retain moisture between rains.

items.symptom: Leaves turn pale yellow or blotchy
items.cause: Manganese or boron deficiency, or leaf miner infestation.
items.fix: A light liquid seaweed feed addresses minor nutrient deficiencies. Leaf miner larvae cause pale blotch mines in the leaf tissue; pinch out affected leaves.
